# The Quiet Museum

*Notes on sounds that have gone extinct*

For millions of years, the wind that crossed the Appalachians passed through a canopy dominated by a single species: the American chestnut. As recently as 1900, one in four of the great hardwoods across much of its range was a chestnut — four billion trees or so, stretching from Maine to Georgia. Then a fungus hitchhiked over on imported Asian nursery stock, was identified at the Bronx Zoo in 1904, and within fifty years it had found essentially every mature chestnut on the continent. The trunks rotted standing up. The forest fell quiet in a way that took generations to notice.

Here is what bothers me: we preserved the wood. Salvaged barn beams, fence posts, coffins, coffers — the chestnut is still everywhere in eastern material culture. Its stump sprouts continue to push up shoots from surviving roots today, and those shoots grow leaves before the blight kills them again. You can go find a chestnut sapling and crumple its slender, saw-toothed foliage in your hand right now. But the sound those leaves made — four billion of them, eighty feet up, struck by a November gust moving through a mile-deep hollow — does not exist anywhere on Earth, and no mechanism existed to save it. Anatomy was archived. Acoustics were not.

We treat extinction as a visual problem. There are drawer after drawer of specimens: skins, skulls, pressed plants, watercolor plates painted by careful hands before the end came. But a living thing is not just a shape. It occupies sound the way it occupies habitat, and almost nothing has been done about the sounds that disappear. Which means the real inventory of what we've lost is longer than the official one.

Consider the passenger pigeon. By reasonable estimates the most numerous bird that has ever lived, at least three or four billion of them in 1800, nesting in colonies so vast that branches snapped under the combined weight. John James Audubon watched a single migrating flock in Kentucky in 1813 and calculated that it passed overhead — unbroken — for three days. People talked about the approach of these flocks the way people talk about weather, because the effect was meteorological: the beating of billions of wings arrived ahead of the birds as a distant rolling roar, like surf or a coming storm, and daylight dimmed at noon when the sky was full. From billions to zero took about half a century. The last one, a captive bird named Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914, and her taxidermied body sits in the Smithsonian. The roar she belonged to cannot be reconstructed from anything. It is simply gone — possibly the largest regularly recurring sound made by living beings on this continent, and unrecoverable.

Humans have also extinguished sounds deliberately, which is its own troubling genre. For two centuries, Europe's most celebrated singers were castrati — boys operated on before puberty so that their adult bodies would carry child-sized larynxes, producing an eerie fused instrument of soprano range and adult lung power. In some years, thousands of Italian boys were cut for the trade. The most famous of them, Farinelli, commanded fees that embarrassed princes, and for nearly a decade he sang the same small repertoire of arias, night after night, to soothe the melancholy of King Philip V of Spain. None of it survives. Not a syllable. The phonograph arrived a generation too late for castrato opera, and the only recordings of any castrato whatsoever are a handful of shellac discs made in the Vatican in 1902 and 1904 featuring Alessandro Moreschi — a sincere, middle-aged chapel singer already considered old-fashioned, captured on a machine barely up to the job. There are extensive paper records of Farinelli's contract negotiations and virtually nothing of his actual voice. Paperwork outlasted pitch.

Some sounds die with their makers; others die first. Blue and fin whale calls are among the loudest sounds made by any animal, and their lowest frequencies ride a natural channel in the deep ocean that lets them propagate extraordinary distances — in favorable conditions, across entire basins, which is why Cold War submarine-listening arrays kept picking up whales no one was looking for. But engine ships fill the low frequencies with propeller rumble, and researchers measuring ambient ocean noise have documented a dramatic rise in the background floor since mid-century, concentrated exactly where whales speak. The result is a strange new category of loss: the animals still swim, the genes persist, but the acoustic room in which a blue whale's call could be *heard* — in some shipping corridors — has contracted from an ocean to something like a hallway. An audience that spanned a hemisphere, reduced until only nearby whales remain. Biologists argue about whether this constitutes extinction; the whales, presumably, have begun to suspect it.

Even silence, it turns out, was a resource. The acoustic ecologist Gordon Hempton spent years hunting the last true quiet in Washington State — meaning not absence of sound, which nature abhors, but absence of *engines* — and found how rare those conditions had become: even in the wettest folds of Olympic National Park, commercial aviation threads overhead every few minutes, most of it carrying passengers to see wildernesses like the one they're drowning out. Natural silence requires thousands of protected acres and functioning atmosphere. It now exists in fewer places than many endangered species do.

And then there is the Kauaʻi ʻōʻō, which I cannot leave out because it holds, as far as I'm concerned, the saddest recording ever made.

The ʻōʻō was a sooty-black nectar-sipper with yellow thigh tufts and a curved bill, confined over its last decades to the sodden Alakaʻi wilderness on Kauaʻi, driven upslope by habitat loss and by introduced mosquitoes carrying avian malaria. Like its relatives, it lived and sang as a mated pair: the duet was the unit of the song, male phrase answering female phrase, call and response stitched into one fabric. Habitat, mosquitoes, then hurricanes wore the population down to nothing, and by 1987 the last confirmed bird on Earth was a single male, moving through the Plateau, singing.

You can hear him. The recording lives in an archive at Cornell. On the tape, his voice is clear and slightly fluted, rising and falling — and this is the unbearable part, the part that turns the file from documentation into tragedy: several biologists who knew the species believed the song cycles he delivers are ones that originally required both members of a pair. He sings the answering parts too. Every few seconds the recording opens into a gap where a mate's reply belongs, and nothing comes, and then he continues. He is performing a duet written for two into absolute emptiness, and he does it correctly, note for note, because that is the only performance he knows. When he went, an entire avian family — Mohoidae, found nowhere else on the planet, ever — went with him. Species extinctions are counted in columns. This one took a whole limb off the tree of life, and the sound of a second voice is what fell.

I think about all of this most evenings, actually, in an embarrassing way. Tonight there will be wind in ordinary trees — oak, maple, pine, none of them rarer than dirt — and it will make a completely ordinary sound. It is tempting to say we should treasure it because it too might vanish, but that frames everything as loss waiting to happen, which gets exhausting. Better, I think, to say what the archives quietly imply: that most of the grand sounds in history were never heard on purpose. Nobody listened to four billion chestnut leaves with intent, or followed a pigeon storm for its own sake, or stood under a pass to hear what continents of wings weigh. They had the greatest sonic events of the Holocene happen on top of them and complained about the inconvenience.

So consider this permission slip, from someone with no authority to issue one: go listen to something alive. Attend, on purpose, the second-to-last performance. Most of what remains hasn't been recorded either — and some of it won't be, but right now it's happening, thoroughly, for free, and unlike Farinelli, you are still in a position to be in the room.

- Elevator music and muzak as a cultural artifact
- The concept of "sonder" — the realization that every passerby has a full inner life

Then the blight arrived and within ~50 years, essentially all of them were dead or reduced to stumps that keep sprouting and dying. Nobody alive today has heard a mature chestnut forest in wind. What did it sound like? We have no recordings. The leaves were supposedly long, narrow — they would have rustled differently than oaks. And now that sound is extinct. Along with billions of passenger pigeons whose wingbeats reportedly made a thunderous sound.

- The chestnut forest wind
- Passenger pigeon wingbeats (Audubon described the sound)
- The Kauaʻi ʻōʻō — the last bird of its species was a male who sang courtship songs to females who would never come. Recorded in 1987. He sang a duet part with only his half. That recording exists but the bird doesn't.

- Dead languages spoken aloud — like Babylonian, we reconstruct pronunciation but can't verify
- The sound of pre-industrial silence — actual quiet. Now quiet places still have distant planes. Gordon Hempton says he searched for natural silence in Washington's Olympic Peninsula and found maybe a dozen spots; even those get aircraft noise.
- Whale songs before mechanized shipping noise filled the oceans — louder, clearer, traveling farther when oceans were acoustically empty

**American chestnut**: Castanea dentata. Blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) arrived via imported Asian chestnuts around 1904 at the Bronx Zoo area. Range from Maine to Georgia, ~3.5–4 billion trees. Made up about 25% of canopy hardwoods in Appalachia. Straight-grained, rot-resistant wood used for everything from barns to coffins. The stumps keep sending up sprouts which get infected before maturity — so the species persists technically but functionally the mature tree is gone. Sound of a forest: we can guess — the leaves are willow-like, long and serrated, narrower than oak. Trees were massive (up to 100+ feet, sometimes more).

**Passenger pigeons**: Ectopistes migratorius. Estimates of 3–5 billion birds, possibly 40% of North America's birds. Flocks a mile wide, hours passing overhead. Audubon saw a flock in Kentucky 1813 that he said passed for three days straight. Their takeoffs/landings were described as thunderous, like a storm.
